newsitem.title: BELGIUM: No Nordic EU bloc seen two years after enlargement.
newsitem.headline: No Nordic EU bloc seen two years after enlargement.

text.p: To the relief of some in the European Union, the entry of Finland and Sweden two years ago did not herald the creation of a "Nordic bloc" with Denmark, previously the only Scandinavian EU member.
As the EU prepares for this week's crucial summit in Dublin on Friday and Saturday, it has become clear that the three Nordic states display sharply different attitudes towards closer integration.
Ahead of the enlargement on January 1, 1995, there had been some nervousness that the entry of the two new Nordics would further dilute the EU by being sceptical towards integration.
There was also concern in southern member states about a possible Nordic bloc making northern European views much more dominant in the EU.

But the three Nordic countries' divergence of views has become especially evident over plans to create a common EU currency in 1999, a key topic during the summit and the bloc's most ambitious undertaking yet.
While Finland is keen to be in the first wave of countries joining economic and monetary union (EMU), the other two Nordics are much more sceptical.
Denmark has already decided not to join and a new referendum would be needed to overturn that decision.
Sweden has not yet made up its mind but many believe it will decide next autumn to wait, even if it looks as though it could meet the necessary economic criteria on government debt and borrowing.

"Things are gradually changing and we are becoming more European, but the feeling of staying outside and seeing how we get on goes deep," said Jan Herin, chief economist at the Swedish Employers' Confederation.

In another key area, Sweden and Finland last week expressed overall satisfaction with a draft paper from the Irish EU presidency for a revised treaty, designed to prepare the Union for eastern enlargement.
But Denmark, which has a history of coolness towards the EU, signalled it had problems with parts of the draft in areas where it may have to hand over more powers to Brussels.
"Both Finland and Sweden are more in favour of integration than Denmark," another Nordic EU diplomat said.
These differences between the Nordics are largely explained by domestic political realities.
"They have different constraints," one EU diplomat said.

This is especially true for Denmark which has opt-outs from key areas such as monetary union, defence, policing and citizenship arrangements, which it won after the Danes rejected the EU's Maastricht treaty in a 1992 referendum.

In addition, a non-partisan group of 11 Danes has filed suit against the government, saying Denmark's ratification of EU treaties could contravene a clause in the constitution limiting how much national sovereignty may be ceded abroad.
Sweden has no opt-outs from closer co-operation but faces strong EU scepticism from both the population in general and from inside the ruling Social Democratic party.
"They are also hostage to a very hostile public," one EU official said. "I don't believe the government has fully understood how dangerous it is to be taken hostage by the nay-sayers."
But Finland seems to have had fewer problems in adjusting to membership. "They normally position themselves right in the centre," the EU official said.

A main objective for many in Finland, which shares a long Russian border, in joining the EU was to boost security and this may explain the fact that it has had less domestic controversy over the EU than nearby Sweden, diplomats said.
But they also underline that Stockholm, Copenhagen and Helsinki have much in common, notably in pushing for strong EU action on the environment, enlargement, employment and openness.
